performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: A single D sounds, and the choir answers almost under its breath. Louis Frémaux conducts an opening built from low strings, long-held chords and a tenor melody that returns as the Kyrie.

sections.label: A · A single D, then the choir
B · The tenors’ prayer
sections.mNote: Tenor melody over violas, cellos, basses and organ

sections.label: C · Winds announce the soprano prayer
B′ · Three voices share the Kyrie
sections.mNote: The tenor melody returns in choral unison

sections.label: B″ · The final Kyrie, pianissimo
sections.mNote: Quiet choral phrases above moving cellos and basses

cues.title: One note, six voices
cues.text: Bassoons, horns and low strings sound D, fortissimo, then let it fade. The choir answers pianissimo in six parts on a D minor chord. The violins are silent. Even the organ waits.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 1–4: opening D, six-part choir, and rests in the violin and organ parts. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Madeleine, January 1888
cues.text: The first performance belongs to a funeral service at the Madeleine in Paris. On 16 January 1888 Fauré conducts five movements for the funeral of Joseph Lesoufaché, an architect. The boy soprano is Louis Aubert, later a composer himself.
cues.evidence: Première, occasion and treble soloist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9). Aubert’s subsequent career: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Aubert

cues.title: The tenors find a melody
cues.text: The marking changes to Andante moderato. Violas and cellos begin to move, and the tenors sing a gently falling melody over them. The organ joins with its soft foundation stops; the horns and bassoons rest.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 5–9: Andante moderato, tenor melody and organ registration Fonds de 8 pieds.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Winds before the sopranos
cues.text: Bassoons, horns and trumpets sound a brief, strong chord before the soprano prayer. The organ adds reed stops, then withdraws to its foundations. “Te decet hymnus” — praise is due to you — unfolds over gently moving violas and cellos.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 10–12: wind chords, organ registrations Anches et fonds and Fonds, and the soprano Te decet hymnus.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cry to be heard
cues.text: “Exaudi” — hear — brings the whole choir to fortissimo. The answer is immediately softer. Fauré keeps alternating the loud appeal and the quiet reply while violas and cellos press ahead beneath the voices.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 13–15, rehearsal F: alternating ff and p in the choir and lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tenor tune shared
cues.text: The Kyrie uses the tenors’ earlier tune. Sopranos, altos and tenors now sing it together in unison, before it opens into four-part harmony. The bass line keeps walking underneath.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 16–17: unison Kyrie followed by four-part writing; the melody recalls pp. 5–6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Christe, then an echo
cues.text: The first “Christe” is fortissimo, the next piano. The choir repeats this call and echo above restless violas and cellos. The organ’s reed stops add bite to the louder appeal.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 18–19: ff and p alternation, with Anches et fonds in the organ.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet final Kyrie
cues.text: The choir returns to “Kyrie eleison” in short, quiet phrases. Cellos and basses continue beneath it; towards the end, a bassoon and a horn add soft solo lines. The last chord is D minor.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 19–22: final Kyrie, dolce wind solos and D minor close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The held chord begins to walk
transitions.from: A · A single D, then the choir
transitions.how: A fermata holds the choir’s last chord. Andante moderato then quickens the D minor prayer: violas and cellos begin their flowing lines, the bass starts moving and the organ enters with eight-foot foundation stops. The tenors take the melody alone, marked dolce espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 4–5: fermata, new tempo, organ registration and tenor entry.

transitions.title: Winds announce the next prayer
transitions.to: C · Winds announce the soprano prayer
transitions.how: Bassoons, horns and trumpets return with strong chords over the low strings. The organ briefly adds reed stops, then restores its quieter foundations at rehearsal E. The strings diminish, leaving room for the sopranos’ “Te decet hymnus”.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 10–11: wind chords, diminuendo, changes of organ registration and soprano prayer.

transitions.title: The whole choir calls out
transitions.from: C · Winds announce the soprano prayer
transitions.how: The strings crescendo beneath the end of the soprano prayer. At rehearsal F the whole choir calls “Exaudi” fortissimo over a D minor chord. Violas, cellos and basses answer with forceful rising figures; the next choral appeal drops immediately to piano.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 12–13: crescendo into rehearsal F and the alternating ff and p appeals.

transitions.title: The tenor melody becomes the Kyrie
transitions.to: B′ · Three voices share the Kyrie
transitions.how: The full choir diminishes and the wind chords fade. Sopranos, altos and tenors begin the Kyrie in unison on the earlier tenor melody, with D still beneath them in the bass. Violas and cellos recover their flowing accompaniment; the vocal marking is dolce espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 15–16: diminuendo at G and unison Kyrie over the lower strings.

transitions.title: The choir strikes Christe
transitions.from: B′ · Three voices share the Kyrie
transitions.how: The Kyrie grows into the first “Christe”, marked fortissimo. The organ adds reeds to its foundation stops, and the lower strings climb beneath the choir. A piano repetition follows straight away, then another fortissimo call: the new words arrive in sharply separated appeals.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 17–19: crescendo, Christe calls and Anches et fonds in the organ.

transitions.title: The last Kyrie settles
transitions.how: The “Christe” calls diminish into the final Kyrie. The choir sings quietly above moving cellos and basses, with the organ back on foundation stops. The lower-string phrases continue towards the final D minor chord, marked pianissimo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 19–22: final Kyrie and quiet D minor conclusion.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: I. Introït et Kyrie, printed pp. 1–22: low strings, bassoons and horns at the opening; organ at the tenor prayer; trumpets in the later wind chords. The violins rest throughout.

timeline.note: Bassoons, horns and low strings strike D. The six-part choir enters pianissimo; the organ is silent.
The tenors sing over low strings. The organ enters on its foundation stops.
Bassoons, horns and trumpets sound forte chords, each marked to diminish.
The sopranos sing “Te decet hymnus” above violas and cellos. Bassoons and horns join quietly at the phrase’s end.
The choir cries “exaudi” fortissimo. Strings press forward beneath soft wind chords.
The wind chords fade. The choir begins the Kyrie in unison, borrowing the earlier tenor melody.
Voices, low strings and organ carry the Kyrie. The winds rest.
Pianissimo bassoon, horn and trumpet chords accompany the choir’s “Christe” calls.
The last Kyrie is pianissimo. Violas hold their notes while cellos and basses move beneath them.
A bassoon and horn add gentle lines to the choir’s last phrases.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.
alts: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.44 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 1 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+40 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.48 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: He spent his days at the organ and in the classroom, saving for songs and chamber music the harmonies nobody else could quite imagine.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
The boy kept slipping into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and the little instrument in its chapel gave Gabriel Fauré his first musical happiness. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he lived among plainchant, organ exercises and the interweaving voices of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was done, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers far outside their syllabus. Fauré acquired a teacher, a champion and a friend who would stay beside him for sixty years. He left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine: a French prayer unfolding over a flowing keyboard part, each new choral entry joining a phrase already under way.
